explanations.explanation: Simon Peter says it plain: "I am going fishing." (John 21:3) And the others don't even stop to think. They answer, "We will go with you," and off they go to the boat. I'd love to have friends who say yes that fast when I say I'm heading out.

Jerusalem is a good guess, friend, but this scene happens by the Sea of Tiberias (John 21:1). Nobody packs a bag for a long walk here. Peter says, "I am going fishing," and that's the plan (John 21:3).

No mountain in this scene, friend. They're by the Sea of Tiberias (John 21:1), and Peter's plan is right there at the water. He says, "I am going fishing," and the others say, "We will go with you." (John 21:3)
Nothing. The text says they "caught nothing that night." (John 21:3) That's a whole night of work with an empty net to show for it. I think that boat had some quiet morning faces on it.
Plenty comes later, friend, but not yet. This part of the story says they "caught nothing that night." (John 21:3) The big catch is still coming, and it doesn't come from their own night of work.
Dozens would've made for a happy trip home, but that's not how the night went. John says they "caught nothing that night." (John 21:3) Not a dozen, not even one. The fish come later in the story.

He calls out, "Children, do you have any fish?" (John 21:5) Simple question, and the answer is a short one: "No." Notice the disciples still don't know who's asking (John 21:4). A stranger on the shore, a question about the catch, and the whole morning is about to change.
That's not what He asks, friend. He calls from the shore, "Children, do you have any fish?" (John 21:5) It's about their night of fishing, and they answer with one word: "No."

explanations.answer: If He can use their boat
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, since Jesus used a boat before, but that's not what happens here. This time He's on the shore, and He calls out, "Children, do you have any fish?" (John 21:5) The disciples answer, "No."

True. They tell Him they have no fish, and He says, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." (John 21:6) Short instruction, big result. I think it's something to see that they do it, since they still don't know who He is (John 21:4).

It's actually true, friend. The disciples answer "No" when He asks about fish, and then He tells them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." (John 21:5-6) They cast it there, and that's when the net fills up.

explanations.answer: They can't with so many fish
explanations.explanation: That's it. They cast the net where He said, and they "were unable to haul it in because of the great number of fish." (John 21:6) Empty all night, then too full to lift. That's a whole new problem, and a good one to have.

Empty was the whole night, friend, but that changes here. After they cast on the right side, they "were unable to haul it in because of the great number of fish." (John 21:6) The net is so full they can't pull it up.

A net that full sounds like it should rip, doesn't it? But that's not what happens here. They're "unable to haul it in because of the great number of fish." (John 21:6) And later John points out that the net was not torn (John 21:11).

Right. "The disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, 'It is the Lord!'" (John 21:7) The text doesn't name him here, so I won't either. What matters is that he looks at that full net and knows who's on the shore.
Thomas is in the boat, friend, listed right there in John 21:2. But he's not the one who speaks up. It's "the disciple whom Jesus loved" who tells Peter, "It is the Lord!" (John 21:7)
Nathanael is in the boat with the others (John 21:2), but he's not the one who says it. John writes that "the disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, 'It is the Lord!'" (John 21:7)

Not quite, friend. Peter does the opposite of staying put. "As soon as Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment (for he had removed it) and jumped into the sea." (John 21:7) The net can wait. He's heading for the shore.

False is right. Peter doesn't stay in the boat. The text says he "put on his outer garment (for he had removed it) and jumped into the sea." (John 21:7) He hears "It is the Lord!" and moves, no waiting around.

Careful with this one, friend. The text says they were "not far from land, only about a hundred yards." (John 21:8) That's nowhere near a mile. The others bring in the boat and drag the net full of fish behind them.
False is right. John says they were "not far from land, only about a hundred yards." (John 21:8) That's a short trip, not a mile. The others bring the boat in and drag the net of fish ashore.

Close, but Jesus says just the opposite. He tells them, "Bring some of the fish you have just caught." (John 21:10) There's already fish on the fire (John 21:9), and He still asks for theirs. I think that says something nice about how He includes them.

False is right. Even with fish already on the fire (John 21:9), Jesus says, "Bring some of the fish you have just caught." (John 21:10) He doesn't tell them to sit it out. He asks them to bring some of their own catch.
That's the number. John writes that the net "was full of large fish, 153." (John 21:11) Somebody counted those fish, friend. I get that, because I'd count my cookies too.
120 is close to a number that shows up elsewhere in the Bible, but not in this net. John says it was "full of large fish, 153." (John 21:11) That's the count.
That's a nice round number, but John gets more exact. The net "was full of large fish, 153." (John 21:11) Not 200, just 153, and the text says they were large fish too.
Torn is it. "Even with so many, the net was not torn." (John 21:11) 153 large fish is a lot of weight for one net. John makes a point of telling us it held.
Tangled sounds like a fair guess with that many fish, but it's not what John says. He writes that "even with so many, the net was not torn." (John 21:11) The net held up.
Sinking makes sense when you picture that load, but the text talks about the net, not a boat going down. John says, "even with so many, the net was not torn." (John 21:11) That's the word you wanted.

Jesus Himself. "Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and He did the same with the fish." (John 21:13) He called them to breakfast, and then He's the one who serves them. I think that's a pretty humble way to start a morning.

Peter has plenty to do this morning, like jumping in the sea and dragging the net (John 21:7, 11), but he's not the one serving. John says, "Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and He did the same with the fish." (John 21:13)
Nathanael is there, listed in John 21:2, but he's not the one who hands out the food. It's Jesus who "came and took the bread and gave it to them, and He did the same with the fish." (John 21:13)

Third. John says, "This was now the third time that Jesus appeared to the disciples after He was raised from the dead." (John 21:14) So this isn't the first time they've seen Him. The word "now" tells us it's one more in a row.
Second is a good guess, but John counts one more than that. He writes, "This was now the third time that Jesus appeared to the disciples after He was raised from the dead." (John 21:14)

Fourth is one too many, friend. John says, "This was now the third time that Jesus appeared to the disciples after He was raised from the dead." (John 21:14) So this breakfast by the sea is number three.
